title: Maple Pecan Granola
subtitle: Toasted oats, pecans, and seeds with real maple syrup
excerpt: Homemade granola costs a fraction of shop-bought, takes thirty minutes in the oven, and fills the kitchen with the kind of smell that makes the whole morning feel different. Pecans and maple syrup are a natural pair, both have a deep, slightly caramel flavour that baking concentrates further. The secret to clusters is leaving it completely undisturbed on the tray until it's fully cold.
sourceNotes: Granola has American roots, developed in the late 19th century as a health food by Dr John Harvey Kellogg and others. The baked, sweetened version popular today, oats toasted in oil and syrup, became a commercial staple in the US from the 1960s and spread to the UK through the health food movement. The maple and pecan combination reflects the American influence on modern British granola.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in a zip-lock bag for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature for 30 minutes before serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Makes a large jar. Stores in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made in a batch and stored. Flavour deepens after a day in the jar.

content.text: Granola is the kind of thing that seems fiddly until you make it once, at which point it becomes a monthly automatic. The ratio that matters is fat to dry ingredients: enough {{coconut-oil}} coconut oil to coat the oats so they toast rather than steam, and enough {{maple-syrup}} maple syrup to caramelise and bind them into clusters. Too little of either and the granola stays pale and loose. Too much and it burns at the edges before the middle is done, which is why 160 °C fan is the right temperature, not higher.
Heat the oven to 160 °C fan. Line a large baking tray with baking parchment.

Put the {{jumbo-oats}} jumbo oats, roughly broken {{pecans}} pecans, {{sunflower-seeds}} sunflower seeds, {{pumpkin-seeds}} pumpkin seeds, {{cinnamon-ground}} cinnamon, and {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes into a large bowl. Stir to combine. In a small pan or jug, gently warm the {{coconut-oil}} coconut oil until just melted, it doesn't need to be hot, just liquid. Add the {{maple-syrup}} maple syrup and {{vanilla-extract}} vanilla extract to the oil and stir together. Pour the liquid over the dry ingredients and mix thoroughly with a silicone spatula until every oat is coated.

Tip the mixture onto the lined tray and spread it into an even layer. Press it down firmly with the spatula, the more compact it is going in, the more clusters you'll get coming out. Bake for 28 to 32 minutes until deep golden and fragrant. The granola will look slightly underdone when it comes out of the oven but will crisp up as it cools.

This is the important part: do not stir it. Leave the tray completely undisturbed until the granola is fully cold, at least 30 minutes, ideally an hour. The maple syrup sets into a caramel that glues the clusters together as it cools. Stir while it's still warm and you break those clusters before they've set. Once cold, break into pieces with your hands and transfer to an airtight jar.
Granola burning at the edges before the centre is done: your oven runs hot. Reduce to 150 °C fan and rotate the tray halfway through.
No clusters forming: the mixture wasn't pressed down firmly enough before baking, or it was stirred while warm. Press harder next time and resist touching it until completely cold.
Granola not crispy after cooling: it may not have baked long enough. Return it to the oven at 150 °C fan for 10 more minutes and allow to cool again fully.
Goes soft after a few days: the jar isn't fully airtight. Transfer to a clip-top jar.
Stir in 80 g of dried cranberries or raisins once the granola is fully cool, adding dried fruit before baking makes it very hard and chewy.
Replace pecans with walnuts or a mixture of both.
A tablespoon of orange zest stirred into the wet mix before coating adds brightness that cuts through the richness of the maple.
